## What varies: writer, session or digit?

Simple summaries per image (height, width, centre of mass), then the share of variance explained by each factor.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#Building the features

img  <- data$images[,,,1] / 255
feat <- t(apply(img, 1, function(m) {
  on <- m > 0.3
  r  <- which(rowSums(on) > 0)
  cc <- which(colSums(on) > 0)
  c(h = diff(range(r)) + 1, w = diff(range(cc)) + 1,
    cx = sum(m * col(m)) / sum(m), cy = sum(m * row(m)) / sum(m))
}))

#Preparing for analysis

df <- data.frame(meta, feat)
df[c("person_id", "session", "digit")] <- lapply(df[c("person_id", "session", "digit")], factor)

# Variance decomposition
vars <- c("h", "w", "cx", "cy")
res_list <- list()

for (v in vars) {
  ss <- summary(aov(reformulate("digit + person_id + session + person_id:session", v),
                    data = df))[[1]]
  
  # Calculate percentage of variance
  pct <- round(100 * ss[["Sum Sq"]] / sum(ss[["Sum Sq"]]), 1)
  res_list[[v]] <- setNames(pct, trimws(rownames(ss)))
}

# Combine into a data frame and format with kable
res_df <- do.call(rbind, res_list)
rownames(res_df) <- vars

kable(res_df, col.names = c("Digit", "Person ID", "Session", "Person ID : Session", "Residuals"),
      caption = "Percentage of Variance Decomposition for Features")
```

Each row is one measurement taken on every image, and each column is a possible source of variation. The numbers are the percentage of that measurement’s total variation explained by each source, so every row adds to 100.

The four measurements

h: height of the digit in pixels

w: width of the digit

cx: horizontal position of the ink (left to right)

cy: vertical position of the ink (top to bottom)

The five sources

digit: variation because a 0 looks different from a 1, 2, 3 or 4 : variation because different writers write differently session: variation because of the recording session, the same for everyone person_id:session: variation because a particular writer wrote differently in a particular session Residuals: the leftover variation between replicates in the same writer-digit-session

Reading each row

h (height): 62.9% is person. Writers differ mainly in how tall they write, and a writer’s height hardly changes between sessions (only 2.9%). Height is a stable signature. w (width): it’s split between digit (43.5%, since a 1 is narrow and a 0 is wide) and person (40.5%). Writers differ in width too, and again sessions add little (6.8%). cx (horizontal position): digit 31.6% and person 34.4%, so where a writer places the digit sideways is fairly consistent. Session × person is larger here (10.3%). cy (vertical position): this is the odd one. Person is only 10.3%, but person × session is 17.0% and residuals are 57.3%. A writer’s vertical placement shifts from session to session and from image to image, so it is a poor feature for identifying writers.

What the table says overall

The session column is under 1% everywhere. No session is shifted for everyone, so session 4 isn’t an unusual session. This supports treating sessions as interchangeable groupings. Person is large for height, width and horizontal position. Writers differ in measurable ways, and these differences hold across sessions. Person × session is small for height and width, larger for cx and cy. Handwriting shifts between sessions mostly in position, much less in size. Residuals show replicate noise. Large for cy (57%), small for w (9%).

## Do a writer's sessions look alike?

Average image per writer x digit x session (sessions 1-4 only), then compare distances between cells.

"how different do two handwriting samples look, depending on whether they come from the same writer or the same session?"

```{r}
#| echo: false


dist_table <- function(M) {
  d4  <- meta$session %in% 1:4
  key <- with(meta[d4, ], paste(person_id, digit, session))
  Cm  <- rowsum(M[d4, ], key) / 50
  k   <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(Cm), " "))
  info <- data.frame(p = k[,1], d = k[,2], s = k[,3])
  
  sapply(0:4, function(dd) {
    i <- which(info$d == dd)
    D <- as.matrix(dist(Cm[i, ]))
    a <- info[i, ]
    up <- upper.tri(D)
    sp <- outer(a$p, a$p, "==")
    ss <- outer(a$s, a$s, "==")
    c(same_writer_diff_session = mean(D[up & sp & !ss]),
      diff_writer_same_session = mean(D[up & !sp & ss]),
      diff_writer_diff_session = mean(D[up & !sp & !ss]))
  })
}

dtab <- dist_table(X)
colnames(dtab) <- paste("Digit", 0:4)

# Calculate ratio and combine with the main distance table
ratio_row <- dtab["same_writer_diff_session", ] / dtab["diff_writer_diff_session", ]
combined_matrix <- rbind(round(dtab, 2), ratio = round(ratio_row, 2))

# Rename the final row for clarity
rownames(combined_matrix)[4] <- "Ratio (Same/Diff Writer)"

# Render using kable
kable(combined_matrix, 
      caption = "Euclidean Distances and Ratios Across Digits (0 to 4)")
```

Distances are in pixel units, so the absolute numbers mean little. What matters is how the rows compare.

Same writer, different session (about 6.4-7.1) is smaller than different writer (about 7.9-8.8). So a writer’s handwriting is on average closer to their own other sessions than to other people’s. That’s the signal that makes any writer recognition possible. But only a bit smaller. The ratio is 0.80, 0.83, 0.81, 0.81 and 0.80. A writer’s average digit changes between sessions by about 80% of the distance to a different writer’s digit. The gap between “my own handwriting next week” and “someone else’s handwriting” is small. The ratio is almost the same for all five digits, so this isn’t a quirk of one digit. Rows 2 and 3 are practically identical (8.78 vs 8.79, and so on). Different writers are no closer to each other in the same session than in different sessions. So there’s no shared session effect: sessions don’t shift everyone in the same direction. That agrees with the variance table, where session explained under 1%, and it supports treating sessions as interchangeable and holding one out.

A writer’s average digit changed between sessions by about 80% of the distance to another writer’s digit, so writer identity is only moderately more stable than session-to-session variation. Different writers were equally far apart within and between sessions, indicating no shared session effect.

### Compare the variation between the people

Firstly, we will compare all 20 peoples handwriting across one session. The main goal of this exercise is to check whether there are any visible variations among peoples handwriting within a particular session. The first image will compare the people writing the digit 0 in session 1.

```{r}
#| include: false
people_examples <- data$metadata %>%
  filter(
    digit == 0,
    session == 1
  ) %>%
  group_by(person_id) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
par(
  mfrow = c(4, 5),
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1)
)

for (i in 1:nrow(people_examples)) {
  
  image_id <- people_examples$image_id[i]
  person <- people_examples$person_id[i]
  
  display_image(
    data$images[image_id,,,],
    paste("Person", person)
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

From the image above we can see that there are different variations in the way people write the digit zero in the first session. Some peoples zeros are more elongated while others look more rounded. The size of the digit differs from person to person. The digits are tilted in different directions, some peoples zero are tilted to the left while others are tilted to the right.

For a more accurate prediction we will compare the between person variation for a different image in the same session. For this we will now compare the between person variation in session one for the digit 1.


In the image above we can see the that there are clear stylistic differences in the peoples handwriting. A visual comparison shows that some of the digits are more elongated than others. There is a clear difference in the way person 3 and person 20 wrote the same digit. Out of all the people, person 18 wrote a digit that tilts most to the right.

### Comparing the digits within people

The next thing we will explore is if there is variation within a persons handwriting. To do this we will randomly select 3 people and we will compare their handwriting across the five different sessions. This particular section is important because later we will build a Siamese network that will compare whether two images were written by the same person or not. A preliminary analysis will visually help us determine if there are similarities within a persons handwriting.

#### Person 1

```{r}
#| include: false
session_examples <- data$metadata %>%
  filter(
    person_id == 1,
    digit == 0

  group_by(session) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()
```


First, we examine Person 1's handwriting for the digit '0' across five sessions. Visually, the digits display consistent stylistic characteristics; while maintaining an overall rounded shape, they feature a noticeably flattened, vertical edge along the left side.

### Comparing the digits of the same person

Finally, we will assess the within person variation of the different digits. The main goal of this is to assess whether there are similarities between a persons handwriting for different digits. This section is important because the Siamese and CNN networks will be tasked identifying similarities within the different digits.

For this section we will use the same three people from the previous section. We will keep the session constant and we will assess them on session one.

#### Person 1

```{r}
#| include: false
person_examples <- data$metadata %>%
  filter(
    person_id == 1,
    session == 1
  ) %>%
  group_by(digit) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()


```

```{r}
#| echo: false
par(
  mfrow = c(2, 3),
  mar = c(2, 2, 3, 2)
)

for (i in 1:nrow(person_examples)) {
  
  image_id <- person_examples$image_id[i]
  digit <- person_examples$digit[i]
  
  display_image(
    data$images[image_id,,,],
    paste("Digit", digit)
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Visually, person 1's digits are centered on the image, and occupy similar proportions relative to the size of the images. Digits 1, 2, and 3 share a similar curved arc like top loop shape. Digits 1, and 2 have similar flat horizontal strokes at the base.

#### Person 9

```{r}

person_examples <- data$metadata %>%
```

Across individual digits, several structural and geometric shapes overlap: Digits 1, 2, and 3 share a smoothly curved top arch; Digits 1 and 2 both feature a flat horizontal stroke at the base; and Digit 0 and Digit 4 incorporate enclosed loop structures.

#### Person 18

```{r}

  display_image(
    data$images[image_id,,,],
    paste("Digit", digit)
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Person 18's handwriting samples exhibit strong slanted characteristics and angular features: Digits 1, 2, 3, and 4 all feature pronounced rightward slants and sharp, linear strokes rather than smooth curves. Additionally, horizontal stroke alignments appear across multiple numbers, Digits 1 and 2 share flat horizontal base lines, while Digits 1, 2, and 4 incorporate sharp, nearly horizontal top or middle cross-strokes.

### Overall Comments

Visual analysis indicates noticeable variations in handwriting across different individuals. Even when writing the same digit, writers demonstrate distinct differences in shape, scale, stroke direction, and style. However, individual handwriting also displays consistent stylistic patterns; as shown in the previous section, a single writer often applies similar structural and graphical characteristics across different digits.
